An exordium is the opening section of a formal speech or piece of writing — specifically, the introductory part that comes before the main body of the work and is designed to prepare the audience or reader for everything that follows.

Think of it as the "warm-up act" before the main show. But unlike a warm-up act, the exordium is not separate from or less important than the main content. It is a carefully crafted beginning that serves specific, deliberate purposes.

A simple "beginning" and an exordium are not the same thing. What makes an exordium an exordium — and not just an opening sentence or paragraph — is that it actively works to accomplish several goals at once:

It captures attention. The exordium hooks the audience so they want to keep listening or reading. A speaker opening a formal address with a striking observation, a powerful question, or a compelling statement is using exordium technique.

It builds goodwill. A well-constructed exordium makes the audience feel favourably disposed toward the speaker or writer. It establishes trust and credibility, signalling that the person addressing them is worth their time.

It orients the audience. It gives listeners or readers a sense of the terrain — what the subject is, why it matters, and what direction the work will take. After reading or hearing a good exordium, you should feel oriented and ready to engage with what's coming.

In short, the exordium does not contain the argument or the main content. It introduces it. It sets the stage.

The word "exordium" comes from the world of classical rhetoric — the formal study and art of persuasive speaking and writing. Ancient Greek and Roman thinkers like Aristotle and Cicero treated public speaking as a structured craft, and they broke speeches down into distinct parts. The exordium was the first and foundational part.

Classical rhetoricians identified a full architecture of a formal speech:

  1. The exordium (opening/introduction)
  2. The narratio (statement of background facts)
  3. The confirmatio (the main arguments and proofs)
  4. The refutatio (addressing opposing views)
  5. The peroratio (the closing/conclusion)

You'll most commonly encounter the word "exordium" today in three areas:

  • Academic writing and literary criticism, where scholars analyse the structure of essays, treatises, or speeches
  • Legal writing and courtroom oratory, where lawyers are trained in rhetoric and the opening statements of trials function very much like a classical exordium
  • Formal or literary prose, where a writer uses it to describe the beginning of any significant discourse with a somewhat elevated or old-fashioned flair
How It Differs from Similar Words

English has several words that all gesture toward "a beginning," and it is worth knowing how exordium is distinct from each of them.

Introduction is the broad, everyday word. Any beginning of anything can be called an introduction. An exordium is more specific — it implies formality, structure, and rhetorical purpose. You would not normally call the first paragraph of a casual blog post an exordium, but you could call it an introduction.

Preface typically refers to the opening of a book — a preliminary section written by the author to explain context, method, or intent, but which sits outside the main text (before it begins). An exordium is inside the main work; it is the opening move of the work itself, not a separate prefatory note.

Prologue is similar to preface but often used in drama and fiction. A prologue precedes the main action or narrative, often providing background. Again, it tends to stand somewhat apart from the main body. An exordium is more integrated — it is the beginning of the work, not a separate preamble to it.

Preamble refers to an introductory statement that explains the reasons or intentions behind what follows — commonly used in legal and official documents (think of the famous preamble to a constitution). A preamble is closely related to the exordium but tends to be explanatory and declaratory rather than rhetorically persuasive. An exordium is more actively engaged in winning over an audience.

The key distinction of exordium is its persuasive and rhetorical intent. It is not just a beginning — it is a strategically composed beginning designed to do something to the audience.

The plural of exordium has two acceptable forms:

  • Exordia — the classical Latin plural, and the more formal of the two
  • Exordiums — the anglicised plural, equally correct and more commonly used in everyday modern writing

Both are standard. If you are writing in a formal academic or rhetorical context, "exordia" will feel more natural. In all other contexts, "exordiums" is perfectly fine.
The Tone and Register of the Word

"Exordium" is a formal, learned word. You would use it when discussing rhetoric, oratory, academic essays, or classical literature. You would not use it in casual conversation without sounding deliberately theatrical or pedantic.

It carries a slight sense of grandeur — using it implies that the work being discussed is serious and formally structured. It is the right word when you want to acknowledge that an opening is not just a beginning, but a purposeful rhetorical act.

To see the word in action:

  • The senator's exordium was so masterfully crafted that even his opponents leaned forward in their seats.
  • The professor asked the students to analyse the exordium of Cicero's speech and explain how it was designed to disarm a hostile crowd.
  • The essay's exordium raised a bold philosophical question, immediately drawing the reader into the argument.
  • Generations of law students have studied the exordiums of great courtroom orators to understand how to open a case compellingly.
  • Of all the exordia he had heard in thirty years of attending academic lectures, this one was the most disarming.

If you remember just one thing: an exordium is the purposeful, crafted opening of a formal speech or written work — one that is specifically designed to capture attention, build goodwill, and orient the audience before the main substance begins. It is the rhetorical art of starting well.
